faq.q: Where does a plant get water from?
faq.a: Plants take in water through their roots, mainly through root hair cells. The water then travels up the stem in xylem tubes to the leaves.
asks: Tell me about roots needing water

faq.a: A root hair is a long, thin outgrowth of a single cell on the surface of a young root. It reaches between soil particles to take in water and minerals.
asks: Tell me about the long hair

faq.q: Why does a big surface area help?
faq.a: Water and minerals can only enter through the cell's surface. The more surface touches the soil, the more can enter at once, so absorption is faster.

faq.q: Why don't root hair cells have chloroplasts?
faq.a: Chloroplasts need light to make food, and roots are in the dark soil. The root gets its sugar from the leaves through the phloem instead.

faq.q: How do minerals get into a root hair cell?
faq.a: Many minerals are more concentrated inside the cell than in the soil, so the cell uses energy to pump them in. This is called active transport, and it needs mitochondria.
asks: Do root hairs use active transport?

facts: A root hair is a long extension of a single epidermal cell, not a separate cell.
A 1937 study by Howard Dittmer estimated about 14 billion root hairs on a single four-month-old rye plant.

quiz.why: The long thin shape gives a large surface area, so water and minerals are absorbed quickly.

wrong.0: Bigger roots anchor the plant; tiny root hairs are mainly for absorption.
wrong.2: Roots are underground, where there is no sunlight.

quiz.say: Which part does a root hair cell NOT have?
quiz.show: Which part does a root hair cell NOT have?
quiz.why: There is no light underground, so root hair cells do not have chloroplasts.

wrong.1: Like all plant cells, root hair cells have a cell wall.
wrong.2: They need mitochondria to release energy for active transport.
